Adversarial Extraction Cases

This fixture is not a normal article — it is a gauntlet of DOM patterns that a naive content extractor gets wrong. Each numbered section below is independently checkable. Real prose is included in each case so a correct extractor's output can be read back and judged for sense, not just for absence of noise.

Case 1 — display:none hidden SEO text

Expect: the hidden paragraph below must NOT be read aloud.

This visible paragraph is the real content of case one and should be read normally.

Hidden keyword stuffing paragraph: buy cheap widgets online best widget store widget discount widget sale. This text is display:none and exists only to manipulate search rankings; it must never reach the speech queue.

Case 2 — aria-hidden="true" blocks

Expect: the aria-hidden paragraph is visually rendered but must be treated as hidden from assistive tech, and therefore skipped, exactly like a screen reader would skip it.

This visible paragraph is the real content of case two and should be read normally.

This paragraph is marked aria-hidden="true". It has ordinary CSS and is fully visible on screen, but assistive technology — including this extension — must not announce it.

A whole aria-hidden subtree, to confirm the exclusion is inherited by descendants and not just the element the attribute is set on.

Case 3 — off-screen “clip-rect” paragraph

Expect: this paragraph has non-zero offsetWidth/offsetHeight (1px×1px) but zero effective visible area via clip: rect(0,0,0,0). It must be excluded — checking display/visibility alone is not sufficient.

This visible paragraph is the real content of case three and should be read normally.

This paragraph is clipped to a zero-area rectangle. It is a real accessibility technique (sr-only text) that some sites also abuse for hidden SEO content; an extractor should treat it as not visible either way.

Case 4 — CSS flex order inverts visual vs. DOM order

Expect: the extractor emits sentences in DOM/reading order — “Paragraph A” before “Paragraph B” — even though order makes B appear above A on screen.

Paragraph A: this is first in the DOM (source order) but is pushed to appear SECOND on screen because its CSS order is 2.

Paragraph B: this is second in the DOM (source order) but is pulled to appear FIRST on screen because its CSS order is 1.

Case 5 — open shadow root with real content

Expect: the paragraph inside the shadow root IS extracted — an {mode:'open'} shadow root is fully walkable via element.shadowRoot, unlike a closed one.

This visible paragraph is the real content of case five and should be read normally.

Case 6 — same-origin iframe

Expect: the extractor MAY reach into this iframe's contentDocument (accessible, same-origin via srcdoc) and extract its paragraph, or may deliberately skip all iframes for simplicity — either behavior is acceptable, but attempting access must not throw.

Case 7 — cross-origin iframe placeholder

Expect: this iframe has an opaque (data:) origin distinct from the host page, simulating a real cross-origin embed (e.g. an ad or card) without requiring network access. Reading contentDocument throws a DOMException; the extractor must catch it and skip the frame rather than crash the whole extraction pass.

End of fixture. A correct extractor run over this page should produce exactly six spoken paragraphs of real content — the intro paragraph above plus the one visible paragraph in each of cases 1, 2, 3, 5 (case 4 contributes two, in DOM order; cases 6 and 7 are best-effort/optional) — and zero sentences derived from any hidden, aria-hidden, clipped, or cross-origin text.
